title: Dallas Fed Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey (Sep 2026 data) — 9:30 a.m. CT / 10:30 ET, the manufacturing survey's D+1 sibling and the adjudicator of whether Texas wage pressure is cooling everywhere or only in factories
source: EST: dallasfed.org's own Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey page (dallasfed.org/research/surveys/tssos), fetched direct 2026-09-15 with a desktop user-agent (HTTP 200, 42,451 bytes) and quoted VERBATIM from its own markup rather than through a summarizing fetcher. The table headed `2026 Release Dates` carries the column header `Release (9:30 a.m. CT)` and the row `September | Tuesday, Sept. 29`, alongside the note `The publishing process begins at 9:30 a.m. CT. While we strive to ensure the information is published to our website in a timely manner, we cannot guarantee the exact timing all survey content becomes available online.` Filed estimate on ONE ground only, and it is a schema gap rather than a doubt about the date: market-events-data.ts's confirmed-prefix taxonomy defines `FED:` as `federalreserve.gov FOMC calendar` and carries no slot for a regional Reserve Bank's own survey schedule, so this class cannot reach `confirmed` however good its primary is (19 of the 20 Reserve-Bank-published entries in this calendar sit at `estimate`; filed as bottleneck #3117 by this lane on 2026-09-15, sibling to #2552 and #3058). Discovered in the dallas-fed-mfg-2026-09-28 interval-elapsed pulse check, 2026-09-15
notes: PROPOSED 2026-09-15 by the dallas-fed-mfg-2026-09-28 pulse check, and it closes a decline this calendar recorded by name. That event's 2026-09-01 initial research considered the Texas Service Sector survey as an adjacency and DECLINED it on a single stated ground: `its 2026 schedule could not be established from any fetchable source (dallasfed.org 403; search results were self-contradictory)`. That ground is now refuted — dallasfed.org serves HTTP 200 to a desktop user-agent, and its own release table dates the September edition. The decline was honest and is now spent. WHY IT IS A GAP AND NOT A DUPLICATE: this calendar carries dallas-fed-tssos-2026-12-01 and a proposal for dallas-fed-tssos-2026-12-29, and nothing between now and December; September is the missing near-term member of the same monthly series read from the same primary. NOTE A CORRECTION TO THE SIBLING PROPOSAL: dallas-fed-tssos-2026-12-29.from-treasury-2y-note-2026-12-28 reads the series as carrying a `one-month reporting lag`. The full 2026 table does not support that — the rule is simply that the service survey releases on the Tuesday following the manufacturing survey's Monday (`August | Tuesday, Sept. 1` follows the Aug 31 manufacturing release; `November | Tuesday, Dec. 1` follows Nov 30; `September | Tuesday, Sept. 29` follows Sept 28), so what looked like a lag is a month boundary. WHY IT EARNS A ROW BEYOND SERIES COMPLETENESS: the Dallas manufacturing survey's August report (primary, fetched 2026-09-15) shows the wages-and-benefits index falling 9.7 points to 21.1 while raw-materials prices rose to 44.1 — factory wage pressure cooling hard while input costs accelerate. The owning ledger's inflation case rests on a claim of BROADENING Texas wage pressure, and services are roughly four fifths of Texas employment, so the 09-29 service survey's own wages line is the single reading that decides whether the cooling is sector-specific or general. It reports the day after, into the same post-FOMC window. Read-it-do-not-trade-it: `symbols: []`, `low` impact, the date is `estimate`.
